A Handful of Pistachios May Help You Sleep Better, Review Says

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1075 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Could a handful of pistachios before you go to bed really help you sleep better?
  • A review of studies published in Nutrition Research Reviews examines how the nutrients and plant compounds in pistachios might influence sleep health.
  • Pistachios contain several nutrients linked to sleep-related processes, prompting an investigation into whether they might offer benefits beyond their nutritional value.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Could a handful of pistachios before you go to bed really help you sleep better?

A review of studies published in Nutrition Research Reviews examines how the nutrients and plant compounds in pistachios might influence sleep health.

Pistachios contain several nutrients linked to sleep-related processes, prompting an investigation into whether they might offer benefits beyond their nutritional value.

While the findings suggest that pistachios may support sleep, the evidence is inconclusive and warrants further study.

“Pistachios are compelling for sleep research because they bring together several nutrients and plant compounds connected to sleep physiology within one whole food,” stated study author Marie-Pierre St-Onge, PhD, professor of nutritional medicine and director of the Center of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Research in the Department of Medicine at Columbia University Institute of Nutrition, in a news release.

“Rather than focusing on a single ‘sleep nutrient,’ this review provides a rationale for studying how the complete pistachio food matrix may affect sleep-related pathways,” she continued.

The narrative review examined existing research on pistachios and sleep-related biology.

The researchers explored whether the combination of nutrients in pistachios could promote quality sleep.

Rather than identifying pistachios as a sleep remedy, the researchers outlined biological pathways through which their nutrients and bioactive compounds might influence sleep.

“We were particularly interested in pistachios because they are particularly high in phytomelatonin, polyphenols, and carotenoids, which we noted were plant-derived components that had been shown to have sleep benefits in preclinical studies,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“We also noted their high content of tryptophan and vitamin B6, which are relevant to melatonin production in humans,” she continued.

Pistachios contain several nutrients associated with sleep, including melatonin, which helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle.

Other studies examining the effects of some of these nutrients on sleep offer further context.

According to recent reports, A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of tryptophan supplementation found that it may reduce wakefulness after sleep onset, particularly at doses of at least 1 gram (g) daily. However, an ounce of pistachios supplies only about 71 mg, which is much less than the doses examined by the researchers.

Additionally, a 2023 review of dietary polyphenols led by St-Onge identified potential links between plant compounds and sleep outcomes, although results varied across studies.

Neither review established that polyphenols or tryptophan from pistachios specifically affected sleep quality.

“I was not surprised that pistachios may help support sleep, given their combination of nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” said Michelle Routhenstein, MS, a preventive cardiology dietitian at EntirelyNourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“Pistachios provide tryptophan, an amino acid the body uses to produce serotonin and melatonin; vitamin B6, which supports these pathways; and magnesium, which plays a role in nervous system function and sleep regulation,” she told Healthline.

The upcoming review highlights the concept of the “food matrix,” or how nutrients and bioactive compounds interact within a whole food.

Instead of investigating tryptophan, magnesium, or melatonin individually, researchers were curious about the combined effects of consuming them together in pistachios.

Laboratory and simulated-digestion research offers clues about how fiber and plant compounds in pistachios and peanuts interact with gut microbes. However, these findings do not establish that eating pistachios changes sleep quality in real-world conditions.

Broader nutrition research also points to a relationship between diet and sleep.

According to recent reports, A 2021 review in the Annual Review of Nutrition examined evidence linking dietary patterns and individual nutrients to sleep outcomes. The findings suggest a relationship between sleep and diet, but note that more research is needed to determine cause and effect.

In a nutshell, the current evidence builds a compelling case for pistachios as a sleep aid.

However, it’s too soon to recommend pistachios as a sleep remedy, as many factors may affect sleep quality and insomnia.

“Sleep difficulties can have different underlying causes,” Routhenstein noted. “If inadequate intake of these nutrients is a contributing factor, pistachios may help, but they may not address sleep concerns related to other nutrient deficiencies or other causes.”.

Much of the supporting evidence cited in the review comes from studies of individual nutrients, other foods, laboratory experiments, or biological mechanisms rather than from trials involving whole pistachios.

Researchers have also reported significant variations in the melatonin content of pistachios, making the amount in a typical serving difficult to pinpoint.

Additionally, the review received support from American Pistachio Growers, and the corresponding author, St-Onge, serves on its advisory board. Larger studies and clinical trials are needed, ideally without industry funding, to ensure well-rounded results.

Indeed, the authors call for randomized controlled trials examining whether eating pistachios affects sleep outcomes, including sleep quality, duration, and melatonin levels.

“This was a review; we noted that the complete profile of pistachios would make them well-suited to support healthful sleep, but research is needed to evaluate this,” St-Onge told Healthline.

In a recent development, “This is the next step, and something we are actively working on. We also need to better understand what dosage and frequency of consumption would be optimal.”.

Regardless, a handful of pistachios is still considered a healthy choice as part of a balanced diet.

Recent findings suggest that “A small handful, about 1 ounce of shelled pistachios, is an appropriate portion,” Routhenstein noted. “Enjoy them during the day or as a light afternoon or evening snack when you’re hungry.”.

If nutrients like tryptophan help promote sleep, it’s possible that other nuts could yield similar results.

“Other nuts, such as almonds and walnuts, may offer similar benefits because they also contain nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” Routhenstein mentioned.

“Early research is encouraging, but it’s too soon to say how much they might help.”.

Other foods, like turkey, also contain tryptophan.

“For someone allergic to nuts, foods such as tofu, beans, oats, eggs, dairy, and fish can provide tryptophan, which the body uses to make serotonin and melatonin,” Routhenstein noted. “The goal is to meet their nutrient needs rather than rely on one food to improve sleep.”.

Sleep health depends on multiple factors. As such, Routhenstein recommends a personalized approach to getting better sleep, from what you eat and when you eat to addressing any nutritional gaps.

Sources indicate that “I would also encourage regular, balanced meals throughout the day to support blood sugar management, especially for those with diabetes, while avoiding large meals close to bedtime,” Routhenstein noted. “Caffeine later in the day and alcohol in the evening are also worth considering as possible sleep disruptors.”.

TikTok’s Viral Winter Arc Challenge Is the Best Way to Get a Jump-Start on Your Upcoming Year’s Goals

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that between holiday parties, happy hours, and meeting your job’s Q4 goals, it may be hard to motivate yourself to lock in on your goals for the remainder of the year.
  • That’s where the 90-day Winter Arc Challenge comes into play.
  • This time of year tends to be stressful, but the Winter Arc Challenge “helps to keep the stress in perspective and also helps us to not get off track or out of balance with the bigger picture” in terms of your goals, claims Chloe Carmichael, PhD, a clinical psychologist and Women's Health advisory board member based in Fresh York City.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that between holiday parties, happy hours, and meeting your job’s Q4 goals, it may be hard to motivate yourself to lock in on your goals for the remainder of the year. While, yes, you should cut yourself some slack here and there during the busy holiday season, it’s also more crucial now than ever to finish the year strong.

That’s where the 90-day Winter Arc Challenge comes into play. This annual challenge, which originally went viral on TikTok back in 2024, starts October 1 and ends January 1 (but if you missed the start, it’s not too late!). The only premise: Stay locked in on your goals for the rest of the calendar year, whether that’s training for a half-marathon, hitting your Goodreads book quota, or mastering a upcoming hobby.

This time of year tends to be stressful, but the Winter Arc Challenge “helps to keep the stress in perspective and also helps us to not get off track or out of balance with the bigger picture” in terms of your goals, claims Chloe Carmichael, PhD, a clinical psychologist and Women's Health advisory board member based in Fresh York City. Now’s the time for you to “be intentional about your energy and what serves you.”.

If you haven’t started the challenge yet, it’s not too late. Whether you try it for 83 or 30 days, the Winter Arc Challenge will set you up for greater success with your Fresh Year’s goals because it’ll strengthen your self-efficacy, or “your sense of belief in your own ability to do what you say that you are going to do,” states Carmichael. Self-efficacy is strengthened through your own behavioral track record, so if you start meeting goals now, you’ll already have momentum heading into January, she explains.

In a recent development, ready to tackle your own Winter Arc Challenge? Here are some helpful tips to help you make the most of the next few months:.

Maybe as part of your Winter Arc Challenge, you aim to cut your monthly spending in half. But a few weeks after setting this goal, you really go overboard at brunches and parties. Don't sweat it. This is “a completely normal part of the change process,” Carmichael says. Instead of giving up when you encounter a relapse here or there, initiative for bumps to happen, then get back on track.

Sources indicate that so, if you spend too much money one week, instead of falling into a pattern of negative self-talk, replace your thoughts. Carmichael notes to plan a script of what you can say to yourself when you relapse, like: “I can still get back on track and feel good about my goals. This is my moment to restart.”.

Say you’re planning to work out four times a week until the end of the year. If you know the cold morning weather is going to persuade you to stay under the covers and sleep in, be proactive: Book workout classes online every week so you know they’re in your calendar, and you’re more likely to show up. Also, write down your challenges—like the dropping temps preventing you from leaving your house—to keep yourself accountable, Carmichael adds.

In a recent development, picture yourself on January 1 having been successful with your Winter Arc Challenge, then move backward and think about everything that led up to it. If your massive goal was to do a yoga class every week, visualize yourself walking through the snow to get to your Monday night class, or doing a virtual class at home when there was a bad blizzard. Also think about when you almost skipped classes and fell off the wagon, but you used thought replacements to continue reinforcing your goals. Using imagery will help you mentally prepare for the journey ahead, Carmichael says.

Industry observers note that ask around to see if any of your friends are also doing the Winter Arc Challenge—or if they’re willing to hold you accountable. Then, plan regular meetups or calls to check in. “Talk about how things went with a promise to be honest and supportive if one or both of you is falling off,” Carmichael claims. “It will help you to stay consistent when you can leverage your social support network.”.

According to recent reports, no matter when you started the Winter Arc Challenge, you’ll see and feel the benefits of bettering yourself in no time. Good luck—you got this!

Tech Report: Navigating the Unpredictable Ride of COPD

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1303 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, HOOVES THUNDER AGAINST packed dirt as the bull bucks to the left and the rider leans right, tightening his grip on the rope.
  • The unexpected twists and turns of a bull ride may feel familiar to people living with inadequately controlled chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD).
  • Mark H., 60, has experienced the challenges that can come with COPD since he was diagnosed in 2010.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sponsored by Sanofi and Regeneron.

According to recent reports, HOOVES THUNDER AGAINST packed dirt as the bull bucks to the left and the rider leans right, tightening his grip on the rope. Just as he finds his balance, another sudden buck or turn can change the course of the ride.

The unexpected twists and turns of a bull ride may feel familiar to people living with inadequately controlled chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Not knowing when breathing challenges or a flare-up—a period when breathing becomes more difficult than usual that can last for several days—might occur can make everyday life feel unpredictable.

Mark H., 60, has experienced the challenges that can come with COPD since he was diagnosed in 2010. “COPD isn’t easy to navigate, and it can be a frightening condition to face,” he says. “I tried to ignore my diagnosis early on because I didn’t want to believe it, and I didn’t want to think about how it might affect my life. But ignoring it didn’t stop my COPD from making itself known. Shortness of breath was really impacting my day to day.”.

It has been revealed that with support and clinical intervention, Mark was able to better manage his COPD and get back to doing more of the things he loves. Now, he wants others living with COPD to know help is available to manage their condition.

COPD IS A complex and progressive disease that can make breathing more difficult over time.

COPD can be caused by inflammation in the airways that causes damage to parts of your lungs. Patients with COPD may also have chronic bronchitis and/or emphysema.

It has been revealed that people with COPD can experience persistent cough, excessive mucus production, wheezing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. Understanding COPD is important, and recognizing when the disease may not be adequately controlled is critical. Living with uncertainty around flare-ups can carry an emotional weight as well, indicates Corinne Young, nurse practitioner, pulmonary disease specialist, who is the Founder/Executive Director of the Association of Pulmonary Advanced Practice Providers.

Recent findings suggest that flare-ups, also known as exacerbations, are the worsening of COPD symptoms over several days. They can happen to anyone with COPD. During a flare-up, difficulty breathing, wheezing, and coughing can intensify and take longer to resolve. Even one flare-up can lead to permanent lung damage.

Young, who in addition to seeing patients, competes in team roping at rodeos, knows the importance of paying attention to changing conditions—a perspective she brings to helping patients recognize when their COPD may be inadequately controlled.

“The biggest predictor of a flare-up is a previous flare-up, and they start to get closer and closer together,” Young explains. For example, someone may experience a flare-up or exacerbation once every two years, then once a year, then every six months, then every three. “Inflammatory responses in the body drive these exacerbations, and that may lower lung function,” Young adds. That decline can increase the risk of additional flare-ups, perpetuating the cycle.

AS MARK’S COPD became more difficult to manage, it increasingly interfered with the life he was used to living. Shortness of breath and frequent flare-ups made it harder to work, travel, and do as many of the things he enjoyed. Eventually, he made the difficult decision to retire early from his job as a field service engineer.

Even after stepping away from work, Mark continued to struggle with his COPD. “I remember feeling like, ‘Well, I guess this is my life now,’” he claims.

Sources indicate that IN THE FALL of 2024, Mark underwent a pulmonary function test, bracing for bad news. The results confirmed that his current treatment blueprint was no longer adequately managing his COPD, prompting a discussion with his pulmonologist about what to do next. His doctor explained that Mark’s high eosinophil count could be a sign of type 2 inflammation. With this information, Mark and his doctor explored other treatment options, including Dupixent® (dupilumab).

Dupixent is a prescription medicine used with other medicines for the maintenance treatment of adults with inadequately controlled COPD and a high number of blood eosinophils (a type of white blood cell that may contribute to your COPD). Dupixent is used to reduce the number of flare-ups and can improve your breathing.

Dupixent is not used to relieve sudden breathing problems and will not replace an inhaled rescue medicine.

Do not use if you are allergic to dupilumab or to any of the ingredients in Dupixent.

Dupixent can cause serious side effects, such as allergic reactions, including skin reactions, that can sometimes be severe, eye problems, and joint aches and pain.

Please see additional Important Safety Information below.

Mark noticed a difference after adding Dupixent. “I could breathe better,” he says. Now, Mark feels less winded, and he’s doing more of the things he loves. “I’m really grateful that I can enjoy my hobbies more without constantly thinking about my COPD,” he adds.

Sources indicate that for Mark, better breathing started with an honest conversation. Young encourages anyone living with COPD to be open with their healthcare provider, who can explain the full range of treatment options available. “It’s not just inhalers anymore—there are a lot of options,” she notes.

According to recent reports, like bull riders who stay alert to changing conditions, people living with COPD can watch for signs that their disease may be inadequately controlled and talk with their doctor about their treatment options. With the right support, they may be able to enjoy more of the moments that matter to them—including, for some, time spent in the rodeo stands.

KEY SAFETY INFORMATION & INDICATION.

Industry observers note that dupixent is a prescription medicine used with other medicines for the maintenance treatment of adults with inadequately controlled COPD and a high number of blood eosinophils (a type of white blood cell that may contribute to your COPD). Dupixent is used to reduce the number of flare-ups and can improve your breathing.

Do not use if you are allergic to dupilumab or to any of the ingredients in DUPIXENT®.

Before using DUPIXENT, tell your healthcare provider about all your medical conditions, including if you:.

Tell your healthcare provider about all the medicines you take, including prescription and over-the-counter medicines, vitamins, and herbal supplements.

Recent findings suggest that especially tell your healthcare provider if you are taking oral, topical, or inhaled corticosteroid medicines or have COPD and also have asthma. Do not change or stop your other medicines, including corticosteroid medicine or other asthma medicine, without talking to your healthcare provider. This may cause other symptoms that were controlled by those medicines to come back.

DUPIXENT can cause serious side effects, including:.

The most common side effects in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease include injection site reactions, common cold symptoms (nasopharyngitis), high count of a certain white blood cell (eosinophilia), viral infection, back pain, inflammation inside the nose (rhinitis), diarrhea, stomach problems (gastritis), joint pain (arthralgia), toothache, headache, and urinary tract infection.

Tell your healthcare provider if you have any side effect that bothers you or that does not go away. These are not all the possible side effects of DUPIXENT. Call your doctor for medical advice about side effects. You are encouraged to report negative side effects of prescription drugs to the FDA. Visit www.fda.gov/medwatch, or call 1-800-FDA-1088.

Sources indicate that use DUPIXENT exactly as prescribed by your healthcare provider. It’s an injection given under the skin (subcutaneous injection). Your healthcare provider will decide if you or your caregiver can inject DUPIXENT. Do not try to prepare and inject DUPIXENT until you or your caregiver have been trained by your healthcare provider.

Please see accompanying full Prescribing Information including Patient Information.

Learn more about Dupixent at Dupixent.com/COPD.

#75787. ACOG Strongly Recommends Hormone Therapy for Menopause Symptoms

ACOG Strongly Recommends Hormone Therapy for Menopause Symptoms

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (911 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) published updated recommendations for menopause management in Obstetrics & Gynecology on October 15.
  • These expanded recommendations are the most comprehensive guidance to date.
  • According to the ACOG guidance, 50%–92% of females experiencing menopause report VMS.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) published updated recommendations for menopause management in Obstetrics & Gynecology on October 15.

These expanded recommendations are the most comprehensive guidance to date. They include new clinical guidelines for menopause hormone therapy (MHT), nonhormonal medications, and nonpharmacological treatment of vasomotor symptoms (VMS), which include hot flashes and night sweats, and sleep and mood changes.

According to the ACOG guidance, 50%–92% of females experiencing menopause report VMS.

Around 16%–66% of females in the United States report menopause-related sleep challenges, and more than one-third of perimenopausal and postmenopausal females report experiencing depressive symptoms.

“In recent years, misconceptions about the risks of hormone therapy have been widespread, which has made some clinicians reluctant to prescribe it and some patients hesitant to use it,” Bruce Pier, MD, clinical professor and associate fellowship director at the University of North Carolina and collaborator on the ACOG clinical practice guidelines, told Healthline.

Industry observers note that “This guidance offers a comprehensive review of the evidence to support individualized counseling and shared decision making. Our hope is that it clears up those misconceptions and expands access to treatment.”.

The ACOG is also developing companion guidance for genitourinary syndrome of menopause, expected in 2027.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of MHT with estrogen and progestogens (or estrogen alone for people without a uterus) for both VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbance, in individuals who can use hormones.

It also conditionally recommends conjugated estrogen plus bazedoxifene (Duavee) as an alternative for these issues.

According to a meta-analysis from 2021 that was cited by the guidelines, estrogen therapy, with or without progestogens, significantly reduced VMS frequency and severity compared to a placebo or no treatment. A 2017 meta-analysis ranked transdermal estradiol plus a progestogen as the most effective option for reducing VMS frequency.

A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis, also cited by the guidelines, found that MHT was associated with improved self-reported sleep quality. Once again, transdermal therapies showed some of the largest effects.

The ACOG recommends initiating MHT before age 60 or within 10 years of the onset of natural menopause..

Recent findings suggest that it also suggests that the decision to start MHT for VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances should be based on a shared decision making discussion about an individual’s symptoms and the benefits and risks of therapy. Consideration should also be taken regarding an individual’s:.

Research demonstrates that factors such as race, culture, socioeconomic status, gender identity, and sexual orientation can influence how individuals experience menopause and the care they receive.

According to the SWAN study, Black women reported more menopause symptoms than white women but were less likely to be treated for them.

Sources indicate that “This updated document shines a light on these inequities. Clinicians can proactively help right now by asking every patient in midlife about symptoms, rather than waiting for them to bring it up. Long term, we hope this document drives more research funding to understand these gaps and begin closing them,” remarked Pier.

The ACOG stated in the guidelines that, “The available evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against the use of estrogen–progestogen or estrogen-only MHT for the treatment of menopause-related depressive symptoms.”.

It recommends that perimenopausal and postmenopausal individuals who meet the diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder (MDD) or those whose most noticeable symptom is depression should be treated according to depression management guidelines.

Current treatment guidelines for depression include therapy, medication, or a combination of the two.

Psychological treatments for depression include psychotherapy, such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), while antidepressants are among the most commonly prescribed medications.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) for the management of menopausal symptoms like VMS and depression in individuals who don’t want to use MHT or can’t use it.

At the moment, paroxetine is the only antidepressant that is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the management of VMS.

The ACOG also strongly recommends the use of neurokinin receptor antagonists to manage VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances in people who don’t desire hormone therapy or can’t use it.

It has been revealed that there are currently two neurokinin receptor antagonists approved by the FDA to manage menopause symptoms. Fezolinetant (Veozah) was approved in 2023 to help manage hot flashes. In 2025, the FDA approved elinzanetant (LYNKUET) for the management of moderate to severe VMS due to menopause.

Another nonhormonal treatment for VMS that the ACOG conditionally recommends is gabapentin.

According to recent reports, there are various nonpharmacologic treatments that the ACOG conditionally recommends for the management of VMS, vasomotor-related sleep disturbances, and mood changes. These are treatments that don’t involve the use of medications.

The nonpharmacologic treatments conditionally recommended include:.

It is generally recommended that these interventions are used alongside hormonal or nonhormonal medications.

The ACOG noted that there is not enough evidence to support the efficacy or safety of phytoestrogens, such as soy isoflavones, or herbal supplements, which are not regulated by the FDA in the same way medications are for safety, purity, or efficacy.

“Menopause is finally getting the attention it deserves, and this document shows what evidence-based care should look like in this space. It lays out a range of safe, effective options for managing menopause symptoms. My message to anyone struggling with these symptoms is simple: talk to your clinician. You don’t have to suffer through them,” mentioned Pier.

The Man With No Butt

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1888 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, I REMEMBER THE first time I became aware of it.
  • New Coke was a thing people cared about.
  • Industry observers note that I was nine years old.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, I REMEMBER THE first time I became aware of it. Or should I say lack of it.

I grew up in the mid '80s. A magical time. MTV actually played music videos. New Coke was a thing people cared about. And a ginger-headed German teenager named Boris Becker—Boom-Boom, to his millions of fans—became, at age 17, the youngest player ever to win Wimbledon.

Industry observers note that I was nine years old. And obsessed.

Recent findings suggest that while other kids my age were collecting Garbage Pail Kids cards or trying to solve Rubik’s Cubes, I was rewatching VHS recordings of Becker’s matches. I practiced his signature serve motion in front of my bedroom mirror. I begged—actually begged—my parents for the complete Boris Becker starter kit: the Ellesse tennis outfit, the Puma half-top sneakers, and the holy grail itself: the Puma Super tennis racket.

According to recent reports, the problem was, no matter how hard I tried, no matter how much Hi-C I consumed, I could never quite achieve the same explosive spring that made Boom-Boom so spectacular. Then I noticed something about Becker’s serve—the one that earned him his nickname. Most players bent their knees to generate power. Becker did something else.

Sources indicate that he stuck out his butt. Like, really stuck it out. His serve motion involved this pronounced posterior thrust that helped him achieve that devastating topspin and pace.

It has been revealed that I went to the bedroom mirror. Turned sideways. Attempted the same motion. And that’s when it hit me with all the force of one of Becker’s 130-mph serves: I didn’t have a butt to stick out. Where Becker had curvature, I had...continuity. My back just sort of continued into my legs.

Recent findings suggest that reality set in. No bum-bum, no boom-boom.

By high school, I had pivoted to more cerebral pursuits like creative writing and a burgeoning interest in art history. Art history seemed safe—just looking at old paintings and Roman sculptures, right? Wrong. It became immediately clear that every civilization in human history had one thing in common: great asses.

One fateful morning during my sophomore year, I was standing at my locker wearing a pair of saggy-bottomed Gap khakis when I heard giggles behind me. The distinctive sound of teenage girls discovering something hilarious and vaguely cruel.

According to recent reports, “Oh my God,” one of them stated. I froze.

It has been revealed that “He has no butt!” another voice announced with the confidence of a scientist making a groundbreaking discovery. More giggling. Then came the death blow that would echo through the halls of my high school for the next two and a half years:.

Recent findings suggest that sure, it wasn’t the most creative nickname, but it had just enough alliteration to spread like a pre-internet meme. From that day on, I knew “they” knew.

It has been revealed that I RECENTLY TURNED 50. I’m happily married and have two amazing kids. Life is good, but I’d be lying if I said the ghost of No-Butt Bender doesn’t haunt me. As I’ve aged, what little I had has somehow continued to erode. My wife loves me despite my anatomical deficiency but remains perpetually baffled by the lack of rear topography. And what was once giggles from teenage girls is now full-throated hysterical laughter from my 13- and 11-year-old children when they catch a glimpse of me in anything form-fitting.

Industry observers note that recently, Instagram’s insecurity algorithm served me up an ad for Perk men’s clothing. Their website is a gallery of flattering middle-aged bum-shots, but what really stopped my scroll was the pitch for their pants: “Our chinos magically turn even a flat butt into a compliment magnet. Whether you’re 25 or 65, that never gets old!”.

You have to understand—when you have no butt, no pants are flattering. So when Perk starts advertising pants that promise to be so bootylicious you’ll receive compliments everywhere you go, I dared to dream. I did what any man starved for posterior validation does—panic-ordered chinos in every damn color.

Industry observers note that five pairs. Overnight shipping.

The moment the package arrived, I tore it open. I slipped them on, turned toward the mirror, and—holy hell—was that…something? An actual curve? A protrusion? I squinted. I turned. And I practically sprinted to the living room where the family was waiting and struck a pose.

It has been revealed that crickets. Then a full collapse into hysterical laughter.

“I’m sorry,” my wife gasped between laughs, “but those pants are working so hard and getting nowhere.”.

I was tired of feeling like the only person other than Hank Hill to be cursed with diminished gluteal syndrome (DGS). It’s a very isolating condition. But I figured if Perk could build an entire organization around flat-figured men, there had to be others out there, living their lives in quiet resignation.

Close to midnight on a Wednesday, my face lit only by the glow of my computer, I did the obvious: Googled “men with no butts.”.

The search results led me to a Reddit post titled, “Gentlemen, how do you live with having no butt?” This guy laid it all out: approaching 29, finally accepting his glute-free reality, enduring constant jokes from his girlfriend, the whole nine yards of tush-less trauma. But what really got me was his closing line: “Please help.”.

I stared at those two words. They contained decades of my own experience—the loneliness, the confusion, the desperation. This post was five years old, but I didn’t care. I had to reach out.

I woke the following morning to find his response waiting like a message from a long-lost brother: “You seem legit I guess. Sure why not.” We were already bonding!

I asked Ross (names have been changed to protect the in-ass-cent) what motivated him to publicly post about his crisis on Reddit, and he mentioned, “It was a genuine problem and if someone’s got an answer that helps, I was going to be all ears.”.

In a recent development, ross first became aware of his DGS when a friend at the gym dropped the bomb: “Dude, you have no ass whatsoever.” The keen observation sent Ross into a spiral of photographic evidence review. He started examining pictures of himself and came to the only possible conclusion: “Huh, I guess I don’t.” It was his own bedroom-mirror moment.

As for the wisdom he received from the Reddit hivemind, he stated it was mostly people prescribing the usual suspects: sprints and squats: “I was doing a shit ton of those back then and still do,” he told me. Five years later, he reports modest gains: “It’s no dump truck but I’ve got a little bit of cushion for comfort back there.” He eventually broke up with the ass-teaser (good riddance) and has been dating a new lady who actually pinches it every now and then—a gesture that, for men like us, feels like winning the Mega Millions.

But the struggle continues. Despite his Stairmaster devotion, sweatpants still “kind of sag” making it look like he may have taken a small dump in them. Still, Ross gave me the faintest glimmer that improvement was possible. Maybe a guy with no butt could transform it into a bona fide ba-donk-a-donk.

I phoned two lifelines from my past—Jonathan Botts, MD, a college friend who’d become an orthopedic surgeon at the Los Angeles Orthopedic Institute in Sherman Oaks, California, and Derek DeGrazio, Britney Spears’s former physical trainer, who had whipped me into the best shape of my life for my long-ago wedding and now is a partner at Barry’s Bootcamp Miami.

Sources indicate that dr. Botts (who inexplicably escaped high school without a single butt-related nickname) broke down the anatomy: the butt consists of three muscles—the gluteus maximus, medius, and minimus—but it’s the maximus that does the heavy lifting in filling out a man’s pants.

When I asked about the possibility of maximizing my non-existus, he didn’t sugarcoat it. “Here’s the problem: You can’t go from what you are now to just working on your butt and developing a huge butt,” he told me. “People are doing lots of protein intake and protein shakes and bulking up like that. You could get bigger and your butt would get bigger with you. Muscularly. But I don’t know. I don’t think you could take huge leaps with just doing squats and lunges.”.

So basically, I’d need to become the Hulk to grow a butt.

Derek offered an alternate strategy with what he calls the Bender Significant Three™. “I can’t say for certain, but I think No-Butt Bender can become Mild-Butt Bender with squats for foundation, Romanian deadlifts to pop your glute a little bit, and a nice hip thrust,” he said.

Mild-Butt Bender. It did have a certain je ne sais quoi.

Derek, who freely admits he was born with “a great Italian ass,” is my gluteal bizarro from an alternate universe where only perfect butts exist. He told me his seat meat gave him confidence in high school, something I could only imagine by taping Springsteen’s Born in the USA album cover to the back of my pants. Derek played baseball, a sport notorious for its revealing tight pants. “I don’t know if they came to watch baseball or if they came to watch us in our uniforms,” he recalled, misty-eyed.

I hated him. I loved him. I wanted to be him.

But then—plot twist!—just as I began fantasizing about playing shortstop, Derek dropped a bomb: “I started to realize that what was a blessing at one point became also my Achilles heel at the same time. If there is a downside, I wasn’t the fastest guy on the team.”.

Wait. There was a downside to having a butt?

Recent findings suggest that dr. Botts, who describes his own posterior as “bigger than average,” delivered the final revelation: Having a bigger butt doesn’t automatically mean you have a stronger butt. “If you have a small butt, does that mean you have weak glutes? It doesn’t at all. You can have a substantial butt and have really weak glutes.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in.
  • There are so many reasons to watch sports, from the obvious excitement that comes with game day to joining a built-in community of fans.
  • The study focused on people with congenital heart disease (which is a range of structural abnormalities of the heart that someone is born with; an estimated 1.4 million adults in the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

There are so many reasons to watch sports, from the obvious excitement that comes with game day to joining a built-in community of fans. But now, upcoming research suggests it may also be linked to fewer symptoms of depression for one group of adults.

The study focused on people with congenital heart disease (which is a range of structural abnormalities of the heart that someone is born with; an estimated 1.4 million adults in the U.S. live with the condition). But the findings are also in line with many other health benefits of watching sports, experts point out.

While many forms of congenital heart disease can be treated, symptoms of depression are more common in this group compared to others without the disease. The fresh study found a clear link between sports fans with congenital heart disease and those with the disease who didn't watch sports. The findings don't suggest that people should skip proven treatment options for depression in favor of watching games, but they do hint that having a sports-watching habit could give some patients an edge in the mental health department.

In a recent development, experts also say watching sports is linked to many positive health outcomes—not just for those with congenital heart disease. Here’s what they say.

Meet the experts: Thea Gallagher, PsyD, clinical associate professor at NYU Langone Health and co-host of the Mind in View podcast; Jason Andrus, MD, chair of psychiatry, Northwell’s Northern Westchester Hospital; and Navjot Kaur Sobti, MD, interventional cardiologist and women’s health expert, Northwell’s Northern Westchester Hospital.

Sources indicate that the study, which was published in the European Journal of Cardiovascular Nursing, recruited 108 adults with congenital heart disease and asked them whether they watched sports and how often. Researchers also gave participants a standardized questionnaire to look for symptoms of depression.

According to recent reports, the researchers found that participants who attended a sports game in person at least once in the previous year had fewer symptoms of depression than those who didn't attend any sporting events. But those who watched sports on TV or online at least once a week also had fewer symptoms of depression compared to those who didn't watch sports.

According to recent reports, the study didn't prove that watching sports actually lowered the risk of depression—instead, it found a link between people watching sports and fewer symptoms of depression. Still, doctors say there's likely something here.

It has been revealed that "One possible explanation is that sports offer connection, enjoyment, and something to look forward to," claims Thea Gallagher, PsyD, clinical associate professor at NYU Langone Health and co-host of the Mind in View podcast. "Following a team can give people a shared identity and an easy reason to call a friend, get together, or feel part of a larger community.".

For people with regular medical appointments or physical limitations, it can also provide them with an interest and identity beyond being a patient, Gallagher claims. "From a behavioral perspective, depression often pulls people away from rewarding activities, which can deepen isolation and low mood," she says. "Watching a sport you enjoy could be an accessible way to reconnect with pleasure and other people.".

Watching sports "doesn't replace staying physically active, but it’s a great, socially-connected way to enjoy some downtime," says Jason Andrus, MD, chair of psychiatry, Northwell’s Northern Westchester Hospital. "A loss of pleasure can be a major factor in depression and perhaps the thrills of victory, or even the agonies of defeat, experienced vicariously while spectating sports, can help break out of the 'blahs' zone," he adds.

People with depression often struggle with low energy, feelings of hopelessness, and trouble concentrating—and that can interfere with taking medications consistently, attending appointments, and maintaining routines around sleep and physical activity, Gallagher states. "Depression can also cause people to withdraw from relationships that provide emotional and practical support, just when they may need that support most," she adds.

Recent findings suggest that the relationship between congenital heart disease and depression can go both ways, Gallagher claims. "Living with a lifelong heart condition, medical uncertainty, and physical limitations can contribute to depression," she points out.

According to recent reports, that's why cardiologists have depression on their minds, too. "We routinely screen our patients for depression as well as other mental health conditions as part of holistic and effective cardiac care," notes Navjot Kaur Sobti, MD, interventional cardiologist and women’s health expert, Northwell’s Northern Westchester Hospital.

Recent findings suggest that it makes sense that playing sports could have serious benefits for cardiovascular health, strength training, community-building, and boosting longevity...but experts point out that anyone can reap the social and health benefits that come with spectating. "The strongest case is for psychological and social benefits," Gallagher claims. She notes that people who attend live sports events often feel less lonely and have a greater sense that life is worthwhile.

"Watching sports can also create opportunities for shared enjoyment, conversation, and belonging, although the experience will depend on the person and how they engage with it," she states.

According to recent reports, overall, Gallagher claims the findings are a reminder to ask people what they enjoy and what helps them to feel connected. "For someone who loves sports, following a team may be an accessible way to keep those experiences in their life, particularly when illness makes other activities harder," she says.

How a Former Newly introduced York City Caviar Factory Became an Art-Filled Oasis of Calm

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1067 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that it’s late Friday afternoon in Manhattan and Alexis Piqueras has misplaced his phone.
  • A break from our harried digital world was what he was seeking when, not long ago, he set out to buy an apartment downtown, having returned to Latest York after a three-year stint in Los Angeles.
  • Piqueras relaxes in the living area of his Manhattan loft with his dogs, Prince and Bridget; artworks by Wolfgang Tillmans (top) and Giangiacomo Rossetti.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it’s late Friday afternoon in Manhattan and Alexis Piqueras has misplaced his phone. Not that he’s concerned. Bathed in the light of October’s early setting sun, the Spanish-born producer and founder of AP Studio, settles into a Charlotte Perriand dining chair at his Tribeca apartment. The vibe is calm: a mix of warm hues, rich textures, and timeworn woods. Candles perfume the air. And all around us the faces and limbs of figurative artworks seem to join our conversation. “I’ll find it eventually,” Piqueras notes, unperturbed by his absent device.

A break from our harried digital world was what he was seeking when, not long ago, he set out to buy an apartment downtown, having returned to Latest York after a three-year stint in Los Angeles. “Sometimes I need to hide amid the chaos,” notes Piqueras, who has built a busy career collaborating with brands on the order of Louis Vuitton, Celine, and Loewe. His real-estate ambitions transcended any simple notions of an urban oasis. Yes, he wanted peace and quiet. But he also wanted some untouched architectural grit that felt true to the city, in particular his visions of its post-industrial 1970s waterfront.

Piqueras relaxes in the living area of his Manhattan loft with his dogs, Prince and Bridget; artworks by Wolfgang Tillmans (top) and Giangiacomo Rossetti.

A Harold Ancart painting and Prince preside over the entry.

Charlotte Perriand chairs and a custom sofa face off across an Alvar Aalto prototype cocktail table; floor lamp by Isamu Noguchi and seascape by Paul Thek.

Recent findings suggest that he found that in Tribeca. Its warehouses and sleepy streets also reminded him of his time in Berlin, where he fell in love with club culture. His newly introduced loft, located in what had once been a 19th-century caviar factory, retains its original brick walls, timber columns, and wood windows, through which he can view slices of the Hudson River. A previous renovation had made smart use of the 2,500 square feet, carving out a primary suite, guest bedroom, office, powder room and pantry alongside the open cooking/living/dining space. It all just needed to be pared back. “The moment you take away everything, you have all you need,” Piqueras notes.

Working with the Brazilian-born furniture and interior designer Pali Xisto Cornelsen, he stripped back what time-stamped interventions had been made over the years. In the kitchen, they updated the existing high-gloss kitchen cabinetry with white-painted fronts and chunky solid-cherry pulls, also installing stainless-steel countertops and a latest island, trimmed in wood. The walls were coated in Benjamin Moore’s Simply White, the floorboards refinished, and the windows dressed in linen roman shades. “I was conscious of creating a neutral canvas,” indicates Xisto Cornelsen, who removed all the recessed lighting. “You’re gonna feel a certain calm.”.

A David Wojnarowicz artwork hangs above a circa-1960 Knoll console.

The den features a built-in daybed; etchings by David Hockney and photograph by Nan Goldin.

Art introduces faces to that expanse. Working with advisor Joe Sheftel to expand his collection, Piqueras has assembled a sophisticated trove with a focus on works by Queer talents of recent or current memory. Those include photographs by Wolfgang Tillmans, Peter Hujar, and Alvin Baltrop, who documented the pre-AIDS gay revelry of the nearby Hudson River piers. Elsewhere are portraits by Larry Stanton and David Hockney. Some bare bodies, Piqueras admits, have left houseguests blushing. But the intention was never skin for the sake of shock. “It’s a lot about community,” states Sheftel. “The apartment also functions that way, as a fun space for friends and play.” A romantic spirit comes across in still lives (a burning candle by Phoebe Helander) and landscapes ( a Doron Langberg painting of Fire Island Pines). Evident too is Piqueras’s deep love of Fresh York City. “There’s also a narrative of activism—of power and creativity through crisis,” says Sheftel, pointing out works by David Wojnarowicz.

In the dining area, Charlotte Perriand chairs surround a Pierre Chapo table beneath a Paavo Tynell lamp; photograph by Wolfgang Tillmans, still life by Phoebe Helander, and portrait by Larry Stanton.

Displayed above the custom DJ station (aka Piqueras’s little Berlin) are works by Wolfgang Tilmans, Seth Baker, and Issy Wood.

A Doron Langberg painting hangs amidst the kitchen’s reimagined cabinetry; photograph by Wolfgang Tillmans and stools by Alvar Aalto.

Sources indicate that the library features a mix of vintage Scandinavian finds, including a Märta Blomstedt lounge chair, Paavo Tynell pendant light, and a desk and side chair by Axel Einar Hjorth. The large-scale photograph is by Wolfgang Tillmans and the shelves display works by Alvin Baltrop, David Wojnarowicz, Jacob Littlejohn, Peter Hujar, and Giangiacomo Rossetti. Resting on the floor is an etching by David Hockney.

A Hunter Reynolds artwork takes pride of place above Piqueras’s bed; speakers by Ojas.

The primary bath retains the building’s original brickwork.

According to recent reports, elsewhere throughout the interiors, they added custom millwork, including the office’s daybed and wall-mounted desk, the living area’s bookshelves, and the dining area’s DJ station, a corner Piqueras calls his little Berlin. Tapered silhouettes and bevels soften edges. “There are all these happy surprises,” says Cornelsen, who referenced design heroes like Le Corbusier, Joaquim Tenreiro, and Jean Prouvé. Vintage furniture adds to that neutral rhapsody, with choice finds by Pierre Chapo, Isamu Noguchi, and Alvar Aalto, whose coffee table prototype anchors the living area. It is joined by a cast of other Scandinavian characters, among them light fixtures by Paavo Tynell, the upholstered Märta Blomstedt lounge chair where Piqueras enjoys his morning tea, and pieces by Axel Einar Hjorth.

It has been revealed that collecting and decorating, Piqueras has found, are not unlike his daily profession. “Renovating an apartment is a kind of production,” he says. “My skill is to orchestrate.” But it’s a break from the grind that he now gets to relish at home. “Work is insane. The streets are insane. But then I can come here,” he says. “I put down my phone—and then I don’t think about it.”.

A Paavo Tynell pendant crowns the guest bedroom, which features more custom millwork and displays artworks by Precious Okoyomon (left) and Christopher Culver.

A Wolfgang Tillmans photograph takes the place of the guest bath’s vanity mirror.

A Sol LeWitt artwork rests on the den’s custom desk; photograph by Wolfgang Tillmans and chair by Axel Einar Hjorth.

SpaceX could announce $1.5 trillion Tesla merger in December: report

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1003 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Elon Musk’s companies are moving faster than expected on a Tesla-SpaceX combination.
  • Tesla holds its annual shareholder meeting on December 3, and the same directors who would sign off on the deal are up for re-election.
  • It has been revealed that according to Bloomberg’s sources, it’s now a negotiation over price and control, with boards and advisers on both sides involved.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elon Musk’s companies are moving faster than expected on a Tesla-SpaceX combination. A deal could be revealed as soon as December, which would make it the largest merger ever, according to Bloomberg.

Tesla holds its annual shareholder meeting on December 3, and the same directors who would sign off on the deal are up for re-election.

It has been revealed that according to Bloomberg’s sources, it’s now a negotiation over price and control, with boards and advisers on both sides involved. December is the target, but early 2027 is also on the table.

According to recent reports, one of the variables on the table is how many SpaceX shares Tesla investors would receive. So, as expected, this is shaping up as SpaceX absorbing Tesla, not the other way around.

In a recent development, that fits the valuations. SpaceX is worth over $1.9 trillion after its June IPO, while Tesla sits around $1.5 trillion. For scale, the record for a single deal has long been Vodafone’s $183 billion takeover of Mannesmann in 2000, and even SpaceX’s roughly $250 billion purchase of xAI (a private company at the time) earlier this year would be dwarfed.

According to recent reports, neither firm commented. Tesla stock rose as much as 1.9% on the report.

We’ve been tracking this since May, when Musk first floated merging the two companies weeks before the SpaceX IPO. At the time, we called it the fourth time Musk would make a more than $1 billion self-dealing transaction, after SolarCity, Twitter/X, and Tesla’s $2 billion xAI investment that turned into SpaceX stock.

Then, in October, Tesla’s proxy filing read like a board getting ready for a SpaceX merger. Ira Ehrenpreis, who chairs Tesla’s compensation and governance committees, has sat on SpaceX’s board since February. The ballot for the December 3 meeting is limited to re-electing Musk, chair Robyn Denholm, and JB Straubel to terms through 2029, plus a say-on-pay vote and the auditor.

A day later, Musk confirmed that both boards had formed special committees to explore a merger.

The governance piece is where Tesla shareholders should pay the most attention.

Musk owns about 20% of Tesla but controlled roughly 85% of SpaceX’s voting power through super-voting shares, according to its S-1. Swapping Tesla shares for SpaceX shares means trading one-share-one-vote for a firm where Musk’s control is effectively locked in.

And the deal itself pays Musk. Under the change-in-control terms in his 2025 CEO award, the operational milestones drop out and the market cap test runs at the deal price, with earned shares vesting immediately. Based on the share count in the proxy, a deal valuing Tesla at $2 trillion (about a 33% premium to where it trades now) would clear the first market cap tranche on the spot. His 286 million restricted shares from the 2018 package also accelerate on a change in control.

Bloomberg reports that one of the main obstacles is how to ring-fence Tesla’s China business. A JPMorgan analyst described SpaceX’s defense and government work and Tesla’s China footprint as “key dynamics that are at odds with each other” for regulators and shareholders.

It has been revealed that that’s the same matter behind the Wall Street Journal’s July report that Tesla was weighing a sale or spinoff of its China operations, which Musk denied. Giga Shanghai is Tesla’s most productive factory and builds more than half of its cars. It shipped 67,829 vehicles in October alone.

Politics is the other wild card. Congress flipped to Democrats in the midterms, and they’ve said Musk’s companies and his political ties will get a hard look. Bloomberg previously reported the companies want to close before President Trump leaves office.

I suspected that the midterms might accelerate the timeline. The Dems don’t take office until January, and Musk likely wants to move this as far along as possible before then.

Sources indicate that no rational independent board would offer $1.5 trillion (much less $2 trillion) for Tesla. It is a shrinking EV company with a few fantasy projects that are not delivering. But endlessly diluting other stockholders is his thing.

Recent findings suggest that as for the “independent committees”, those are obviously a joke. No one believes that, but it’s not like Tesla’s shareholders would care at this point. Tesla’s stock has been a dud for 4 years, and shareholders’ best chance to see a return is another self-deal with Musk.

Tesla is a car and energy company with falling car sales, and it would get folded into a rocket, satellite, and AI company that’s valued at a premium to it and controlled by one person.

This is the end game. At least, it looks like Elon is running out of companies to fold together to hide underperformance.

If you’re following Tesla because of its energy business, the cheapest way to tap into that transition at home is still putting solar on your own roof. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. Sources indicate that our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

According to recent reports, I’M A SUCKER for a good Barbour jacket. I’ve always considered the British heritage brand’s waxed-cotton outerwear the perfect finishing touch to a nicely put-together fall-winter outfit. Founded in 1894, Barbour originally made weather-resistant jackets for sailors, fishermen, and outdoor workers before becoming a staple of British countryside dressing. Over the years, its association with the royal family, including Princess Diana and King Charles III, helped give the rugged outerwear an upper-class appeal. But in the past five years, Barbour has seen a major resurgence, thanks to the barn-jacket boom on runways at Prada, Loewe, and Bottega Veneta, along with a growing appetite for timeless pieces over fast fashion. Buzzy collaborations with designers like Gucci and Paul Smith, plus the popularity of British countryside style in shows like The Crown, have also introduced the look to a whole latest generation of guys.

But as much as I love Barbour jackets, dropping several hundred dollars on one isn’t exactly in everyone’s budget. Some of the brand’s most iconic styles, including the Bedale, Beaufort, and Ashby, will set you back anywhere from $415 to $450. And that’s before you dive into the designer collabs. Take the latest J.Crew x Barbour Beaufort jacket. It’s a fresh, reimagined take on the brand’s signature outerwear, dressed in a bold apple-green shade with a weather-resistant finish and tartan lining. Personally, it has me in a chokehold. At nearly $500, it’s a pretty steep investment, especially if you’re just looking to dip your toes into the barn-jacket trend.

Thankfully, you don’t have to spend that kind of money to capture the same British countryside charm. Plenty of menswear brands have put their own spin on the classic barn jacket, offering similar silhouettes, canvas fabrics, and utilitarian details at more digestible prices. I’ve rounded up some stylish Barbour jacket alternatives from brands like Bonobos and Quince that look just as sharp, whether you’re getting dressed up or keeping it casual.

Of all the Barbour jacket alternatives I’ve tested, Quince’s version comes close in comparison to the Barbour x Paul Smith collaboration I already own. That jacket runs north of $800, while Quince’s costs just over a hundred bucks but with nearly all the same bells and whistles: a two-tone brown colorway, contrasting corduroy collar, and snap-button storm throat flap that helps seal out drafts of wind. There’s also a two-way zipper that lets me open the jacket from the bottom when I need a little more breathing room.

It has been revealed that it’s made from 100% organic cotton and fully lined with soft cotton flannel, which adds a welcome layer of warmth on chilly days when I can skip wearing a bulky sweater underneath. The cut hits just below the waist, with a roomy fit that leaves plenty of space for layering without feeling overly baggy. I’ve even worn it through a few light rain showers, and the fabric didn’t get soaked. I also appreciate how the classic design makes it easy to dress up with trousers and an Oxford shirt or keep things casual with jeans and boots.

According to recent reports, uniqlo makes one of the best affordable Barbour alternatives I’ve come across, and at just $80, it looks and feels more expensive than it actually is. The lightly padded cotton-nylon fabric provides just enough warmth for temps below 60 degrees. What I especially like is the clean, sleek design that comes with a concealed front closure that hides the buttons and zipper, giving the jacket a sharper, more polished look when fully fastened. There’s also a classic checked lining and two-way flap pockets that can be accessed from the top or sides.

In a recent development, fit-wise, it has a relaxed, boxy silhouette that hits right at the waist and leaves enough room to comfortably layer a chunky knit over a dress shirt. And unlike some barn jackets that lean heavily into the rugged workwear aesthetic, this one feels a little more understated. It comes in versatile neutrals like olive, khaki, black, and dark brown, so finding one that works with your wardrobe shouldn’t be difficult.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re looking for something that puts a slightly different spin on the traditional barn jacket, Bonobos has you covered. Its Canvas Ranch Jacket trades the usual waxed-cotton construction for a sturdy cotton-elastane blend that has a little stretch, so I’m not feeling boxed in. But what really caught my attention are the angled patch pockets across the front. They’re a subtle departure from the usual straight-cut or flap pockets you see on most field jackets, giving the whole design a more distinctive, modern feel.

The cut extends past the waist and lands around the upper thigh, offering a little more coverage than your typical trucker jacket. I also like that Bonobos keeps the color options simple with midnight navy and forest green, both of which go nicely with denim, chinos, or tailored trousers.

According to recent reports, for guys who want the classic Barbour look with a little more protection against the elements, consider this insulated version from L.L.Bean. Unlike some of the lighter options on this list, this one is packed with 60 grams of PrimaLoft Black insulation, a lightweight synthetic fill that helps keep it toasty inside without the bulk of a heavy winter coat. The 100% cotton exterior has a water-resistant waxed finish that will keep you dry in light rain. It also has a quilted exterior that gives the traditional field-jacket silhouette a slightly more outdoorsy vibe.

In a recent development, it’s slightly fitted, so guys who are super jacked might have to size up. But the regular-length cut makes it easy to wear over everyday layers and not feel overly snug. This is a great option for construction laborers, landscapers, and other guys who spend long hours outdoors. It’s more practical than fashion-forward, but you get the timeless look of a heritage field jacket with added insulation and weather protection that make it useful beyond just completing an outfit.

Recent findings suggest that flint and Tinder’s waxed trucker jacket famously appeared on Pedro Pascal in HBO’s The Last of Us, and we’ve been major fans ever since. This is a burly, no-nonsense trucker jacket made from Martexin waxed sailcloth that’s treated on both sides to help block wind and repel light rain. The antique-finish metal buttons and earthy color options give it that rugged, worn-in look that only gets better with age. On the inside, a full-length blanket-style lining keeps you cozy during 50-degree mornings.

In a recent development, one thing worth mentioning is that the waxed fabric feels pretty stiff at first, so don’t expect it to have that soft, broken-in feel right out of the gate. But that’s also part of the appeal of this type of outerwear. After three wears, the fabric gradually softens and develops more character. Compared to Barbour’s longer field jackets, this one has a more traditional trucker silhouette, so I can pair it with jeans, boots, and other casual staples.

According to recent reports, not every Barbour alternative needs to look like it belongs in the English countryside. Case in point: AYR’s The Club, which takes a more refined approach. It’s made from weatherproofed waxed cotton that offers a water-repellent finish. The fabric is also light enough to wear across three seasons, making it a versatile option for those in-between days when a heavy coat feels like overkill.

I can throw it over a tee with jeans for the weekend or wear it with a collared shirt and trousers to the office. I wore it in light showers, and it didn’t soak through to my clothes. And at a little over $300, it’s certainly not the cheapest alternative on this list. Still, if you’re after something that feels more stylish than rugged, this one makes a strong case for itself.

Industry News: Christina Applegate ‘Not Happy at All’ After Learning She Was Misdiagnosed With MS

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Christina Applegate shared an unexpected health update on her return to the MeSsy podcast with co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler.
  • The two actors have detailed their experiences with multiple sclerosis (MS), a neurological disorder that can lead to debilitating symptoms affecting daily functioning and quality of life.
  • Applegate, 54, has been raising awareness about the condition since her initial diagnosis in 2021.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Christina Applegate shared an unexpected health update on her return to the MeSsy podcast with co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler.

The two actors have detailed their experiences with multiple sclerosis (MS), a neurological disorder that can lead to debilitating symptoms affecting daily functioning and quality of life.

Applegate, 54, has been raising awareness about the condition since her initial diagnosis in 2021.

In two podcast episodes released October 20, Applegate revealed that doctors had told her she was misdiagnosed with MS.

“She came into my room and remarked, ‘Congratulations, you don’t have MS,’ ” Applegate said as she fought back tears. “I was, like, not happy at all. Everybody else was so happy.”.

The “Anchorman” and “Dead to Me” actor explained that her symptoms have continued to worsen, leaving her without an explanation for what she’s experiencing as doctors investigate the cause.

It has been revealed that being misdiagnosed with MS is relatively common. Applegate’s revelation highlights a difficult reality for people living with unexplained symptoms resembling MS. Her experience raises questions about how MS is diagnosed, why misdiagnoses may occur, and what people can do when their symptoms don’t match their diagnosis.

Industry observers note that while MS can be difficult to diagnose, an accurate diagnosis can help people with the condition gain access to appropriate treatment. A misdiagnosis, on the other hand, may lead to unnecessary interventions and medication, and take an emotional toll over time.

“MS can be challenging to diagnose because there is no single test that confirms it in every case,” remarked Steve Allder, MD, consultant neurologist at Re:Cognition Health.

“An incorrect diagnosis can have significant consequences. Someone incorrectly diagnosed with MS may experience considerable anxiety, undergo unnecessary investigations, or receive treatments with potential risks and side effects. Equally, if MS is missed, treatment may be delayed, potentially allowing further neurological damage,” Allder told Healthline.

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis underscores that MS misdiagnoses remain a concern.

Research suggests that around 15% of people diagnosed with MS may actually have another condition.

However, estimates vary across studies, with some reporting rates ranging from 5–41%.

While an accurate diagnosis can guide patients toward appropriate treatment, a mistaken one may lead to unnecessary medication, emotional distress, and years of uncertainty.

Latest diagnostic guidelines offer hope for greater accuracy, but they also raise key questions about how doctors can adequately distinguish MS from other conditions.

“Research has shown that MS can be both overdiagnosed and underdiagnosed,” Allder said.

“Diagnosis relies on a combination of symptoms, neurological examination, MRI findings, and sometimes, additional tests. It is also key to recognize that diagnoses can evolve as new evidence emerges. As neurologists, we must remain open to revisiting a diagnosis when symptoms or test results do not fit, ensuring patients receive appropriate treatment and support.”.

MS symptoms may vary widely and overlap with several other conditions. These may include:.

Because these conditions share certain features with MS, healthcare professionals should consider a patient’s full clinical profile rather than relying on a single symptom or scan.

“MS can cause numbness, tingling, muscle weakness, visual disturbances, balance problems, and fatigue. However, these symptoms are not unique to the condition,” Allder noted.

“For example, numbness and tingling may indicate peripheral neuropathy, sometimes associated with diabetes or vitamin B12 deficiency. Weakness or altered sensation may result from a trapped nerve or spinal cord compression. Migraines can cause visual disturbances and sensory symptoms, while inner-ear disorders may affect balance,” he continued.

Allder noted that fatigue is particularly nonspecific and may be associated with:.

He explained that, as a neurologist, he considers the pattern, duration, and progression of symptoms alongside examination findings.

Sources indicate that “No single symptom automatically indicates MS. A thorough assessment is essential to identify the underlying cause and ensure the patient receives appropriate treatment,” he said.

There is no single test that definitively confirms every case of MS.

Diagnosis typically involves reviewing symptoms, conducting neurological examinations, and evaluating MRI scans and laboratory results.

According to recent reports, MRI findings may be tricky to interpret. Some white-matter spots resemble MS lesions but may result from migraine, aging, or other conditions. Misapplying diagnostic criteria or overlooking alternative explanations can also lead to mistakes.

Sources indicate that “MRI abnormalities alone do not confirm MS,” Allder stated. “The diagnosis must be based on the overall clinical picture, with alternative explanations carefully considered.”.

Research also suggests that MS misdiagnosis rates may differ by sex.

Research demonstrates females are 2.1 times more likely to be misdiagnosed with MS than males, highlighting the potential for diagnostic bias and differences in how symptoms are evaluated.

The updated MS diagnostic criteria published in 2025 offer a framework for improving diagnosis.

The updated guidelines introduce several vital changes.

For instance, the optic nerve (the nerve connecting the eye to the brain) is now included as a fifth anatomical location for assessing evidence of MS.

According to recent reports, the revised criteria also include upcoming MRI biomarkers, such as the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions. These features can help doctors distinguish MS-related abnormalities from other conditions.

These changes may help doctors diagnose MS earlier and more accurately.

It has been revealed that if you experience persistent or recurring neurological symptoms, seek medical advice. Your doctor can assess your symptoms and, if applicable, refer you to a neurologist.

Sudden weakness, vision loss, or difficulty speaking requires urgent medical assessment, Allder said.

“Depending on the findings, investigations may include MRI scans of the brain and spinal cord, blood tests, and, in some cases, a lumbar puncture,” Allder noted.

“It is important that results are interpreted alongside symptoms and examination findings, as no single test should determine the diagnosis in isolation.”.

Allder said that if you’re unsure about a diagnosis, you can ask your neurologist what evidence supports it and whether alternative health conditions have been considered.

Recent findings suggest that “A second opinion or follow-up assessment may be appropriate. The priority is an accurate diagnosis that leads to the right treatment and support,” Allder noted.
